notes: Heckfield Wood House phase 1 repudiatory cancellation; section 107 writing and adjudication enforcement.

enrichment.short_title: Heckfield Wood House: repudiatory cancellation of cost-plus phase 1 works

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: AHL began cost-plus phase 1 wind-and-weathertighting works at Heckfield Wood House on 8 September 2003 under letters and a site meeting minute.
The Estate's agent stopped the project on 16 September 2003, leaving most agreed scope unperformed.
AHL claimed about £132,000 loss in a third adjudication; Mr Wakefield awarded £73,400 plus interest.
The Estate sought declarations that no defined-scope construction contract in writing existed and that the adjudicator lacked jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 7 TCC trial following Part 8 claim seeking to resist enforcement of a third adjudicator's decision on jurisdiction and contract formation.
enrichment.outcome: Estate's claim dismissed; AHL's Part 20 claim succeeded and the adjudicator's decision was ordered to be enforced.
enrichment.ratio: An employer could not lawfully omit the entire phase 1 scope once a cost-plus contract to make the building wind and weathertight existed; all express terms were evidenced in writing for section 107 purposes, and the repudiatory termination supported a valid adjudication award.
legal_issues: Whether there was a contract for a defined scope of phase 1 works
Whether the employer could cancel the whole remaining project as a variation
Whether the contract was evidenced in writing under section 107 HGCRA
Whether the third adjudicator's award was valid and enforceable
linked_authorities: Abbey Developments Ltd v PP Brickwork Ltd [2003] EWHC 1987 (TCC)
RJT Consulting Engineers Ltd v DM Engineering (Northern Ireland) Ltd [2002] BLR 217

confidence.notes: Contract scope, section 107 analysis and enforcement outcome are fully reasoned in the judgment.

notes: Fresh Portuguese extradition evidence; mistake of fact remittal under E and R principles.

enrichment.short_title: Cabo-Verde: remittal after undisclosed Portuguese extradition evidence
key_facts: Mr Cabo-Verde claimed asylum against return to Angola, alleging FLEC membership, capture, torture and bribery-assisted release in 2002.
An adjudicator found him credible but excluded refugee status under Article 1(F); the IAT allowed his Article 3 appeal in December 2002.
In October 2003 Portugal sought extradition alleging robberies in Portugal during the same months he claimed to have been imprisoned in Angola.
The Secretary of State sought late remittal on fresh evidence that the tribunal had been unaware of the Portuguese investigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission to appeal an Immigration Appeal Tribunal Article 3 decision, based on fresh extradition-related evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the human rights application remitted to the IAT for reconsideration de novo in light of the new material.
enrichment.ratio: Asylum appeals may be reopened where relevant evidence was objectively verifiable, uncontentious, unknown to the tribunal through no fault of the appellant and materially affected the decision; this is a mistake-of-fact challenge under E and R, not a fraud-based setting aside requiring strict proof of fraud.
legal_issues: Whether delay barred the Secretary of State's appeal
Whether Portuguese extradition material amounted to fresh evidence justifying remittal
Application of the E and R mistake-of-fact test in asylum law
Whether fraud must be strictly proved before reopening a favourable tribunal decision
linked_authorities: E and R v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] QB 1044
Khan v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 530
Asur Saribal v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] EWHC 1542 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Procedural history and E/R test application are clear; underlying merits of the Portuguese allegations were not finally decided.

notes: Renewed JR refusing challenge to Employment Tribunal non-recording practice; natural justice and Article 6.

enrichment.short_title: Matthews: challenge to Employment Tribunal non-recording practice refused
key_facts: Mr Matthews, employer respondent in a redundancy payment claim, failed in the Employment Tribunal and sought to challenge alleged perjury by claimants.
He applied for judicial review of the general practice of Employment Tribunals not to make contemporaneous recordings or full transcripts of hearings.
Tribunals record reasons for decisions but chairs take note of evidence rather than producing verbatim transcripts.
Matthews did not attend the tribunal hearing after an adjournment application was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review of Employment Tribunal practice on recording evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; the challenge was unarguable because absence of recording does not breach natural justice or Article 6.
enrichment.ratio: Natural justice requires a fair hearing free from bias, not verbatim recording; Article 6 is satisfied by a full public hearing of the issues and absence of recording is the norm in most tribunals and county courts and does not of itself render proceedings unfair.
legal_issues: Whether failure to record tribunal evidence breaches natural justice
Whether Article 6 requires contemporaneous recording or transcript of Employment Tribunal hearings
Whether the claimant had sufficient interest to challenge a general practice
Relevance of the claimant's non-attendance and pursuit of perjury allegations

confidence.notes: Short judgment with direct holdings on natural justice and Article 6; no linked cases were material to the ratio.

notes: Formula One Holdings board composition; Schedule 1 shareholder agreement and summary judgment under CPR 24.

enrichment.short_title: Formula One Holdings: validity of A and B director appointments on summary judgment
key_facts: Speed Investments and Bambino disputed the composition of the eight-director board of Formula One Holdings Ltd after Speed increased its SLEC shareholding to 75%.
Under the 12 May 2000 shareholders agreement and new articles, four A directors and four B directors were specified in Schedule 1, including Ecclestone and Mullens as B directors.
Bambino purported to appoint the Argands as B directors in October 2002 while treating Ecclestone and Mullens as ordinary directors.
Speed applied for summary judgment declaring Ecclestone and Mullens B directors and the Argands' and rival appointments invalid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for declarations on FOH board composition with Bambino resisting Speed's CPR 24.2 summary judgment application.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for Speed; declarations made that Ecclestone and Mullens were B directors and the Argands were not validly appointed.
enrichment.ratio: Schedule 1 to the shareholders agreement, read with the new articles and quorum provisions, effectively designated existing directors as A or B directors on 12 May 2000; the Duomatic principle cured trivial formal defects and Bambino had no real prospect of rectification.
legal_issues: Whether Ecclestone and Mullens became B directors on adoption of the 2000 articles and Schedule 1
Whether Bambino could appoint the Argands as additional B directors
Validity of Speed's appointment of Diederichs and Mann as ordinary directors
Whether rectification of the shareholders agreement was arguable
linked_authorities: Re Duomatic Ltd [1969] 2 Ch 365
Euro Brokers Holdings Ltd v Monecor London Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 105

confidence.notes: Corporate structure and documentary construction are extensively analysed; outcome is clear.

notes: Arson-related gross negligence manslaughter; duty of care in joint criminal enterprise following Wacker.

enrichment.short_title: Willoughby: gross negligence manslaughter after petrol arson killed accomplice
key_facts: Willoughby owned a disused Canterbury pub with heavy mortgage arrears and failed planning applications.
The Crown alleged he recruited Derek Drury to help set fire to the building using petrol, causing an explosion that killed Drury.
The jury convicted of reckless arson and manslaughter; appeal was limited to the gross negligence manslaughter direction.
The judge left duty of care to the jury where the owner enlisted Drury to spread petrol in a high-risk arson plan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave, limited to the trial judge's gross negligence manslaughter direction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction safe despite preference for unlawful-act manslaughter route and immaterial misdirection on ownership alone.
enrichment.ratio: Gross negligence manslaughter may coexist with unlawful-act manslaughter; whether a duty of care exists is normally for the jury where there is evidence, and enlisting an accomplice to spread petrol in a planned arson can found such a duty notwithstanding joint criminality, following Wacker on public policy.
legal_issues: Whether the owner owed Drury a duty of care during joint petrol arson
Judge or jury determination of existence of duty in gross negligence manslaughter
Relationship between unlawful-act and gross negligence routes
Whether conviction was unsafe given arson verdict and summing-up focus on ownership
linked_authorities: R v Wacker [2003] 1 Cr App R 329
R v Adomako [1995] 1 AC 171
R v Khan & Khan [1998] Crim LR 83

confidence.notes: Facts, summing-up challenge and Wacker-based appellate reasoning are clearly set out.

notes: Section 142 MCA reopening of dangerous driving sentence; finality and victim injury aggravation.

enrichment.short_title: Holme: magistrates wrongly reopened dangerous driving sentence under section 142
key_facts: Holme pleaded not guilty to dangerous driving but accepted careless driving after hitting a pedestrian on a crossing at excessive speed in November 2002.
On 3 December 2003 Liverpool magistrates sentenced him to 50 hours' community service and a 12-month disqualification.
A victim complaint led the bench five months later to reopen sentencing under section 142, believing fuller injury evidence might have justified custody.
Holme had already completed the community service order when judicial review was brought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review to quash magistrates' decision to reopen sentencing under section 142 Magistrates' Courts Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; the section 142 decision was quashed as an improper use of the slip-rule power.
enrichment.ratio: Section 142 is a limited slip-rule power that may in rare cases permit reopening where the court was materially misled, but finality in sentencing is fundamental; a five-month delay, incomplete ignorance of injury severity and pursuit of a substantially harsher custodial sentence did not justify reopening here.
legal_issues: Scope of section 142 to vary or rescind a lawful sentence
Whether magistrates were misled about extent of victim injuries
Application of sentencing finality principles from ex parte Pierson
Whether serious injury can aggravate a dangerous driving sentence
linked_authorities: R v Croydon Youth Court, ex parte DPP [1997] 2 Cr App R 411
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Pierson [1998] AC 539
R v Stokes [1998] 1 Cr App R (S) 282

confidence.notes: Chronology, section 142 analysis and finality principles are comprehensively explained.

notes: Restraining order breach; abusive actions meaning under Cozens v Brutus and reasonable excuse.

enrichment.short_title: Evans: parking car to block neighbour's guest held abusive breach of restraining order
key_facts: Mrs Evans was subject to a 1999 restraining order prohibiting abusive words or actions towards named neighbours and entry onto their property.
On 4 February 2003 she moved her car forward to block a plumber's van visiting Mrs Edwards next door, trapping it between two vehicles.
CCTV captured the incident amid a long history of neighbour harassment; the jury convicted on one count of breach.
The judge rejected no-case submissions and left 'abusive actions' to the jury without a special narrow definition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction for breach of a section 5 restraining order contrary to section 5(5) Protection from Harassment Act 1997.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge correctly left the ordinary meaning of 'abusive actions' to the jury and no reasonable excuse was raised.
enrichment.ratio: The meaning of ordinary words in a restraining order is for the jury unless a special sense is shown; 'abusive actions' bears its ordinary meaning and applying Cozens v Brutus, blocking a visitor's vehicle out of spite could properly be found abusive, with section 5(5) reasonable excuse protecting defendants who reasonably misunderstand an order.
legal_issues: Whether parking to block a neighbour's guest was 'abusive actions' under the order
Judge or jury determination of meaning of ordinary words in restraining orders
Whether the first limb of the order made other limbs redundant
Direction on reasonable excuse where the defendant did not give evidence
linked_authorities: Cozens v Brutus [1973] AC 854
Moyna v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2003] UKHL 44
R v Parkin [2004] EWCA Crim 287

confidence.notes: Legal framework, fact pattern and Cozens-based analysis are fully articulated by the Court of Appeal.

notes: POCA 2002 Part 5 civil recovery; interim receiving order good arguable case and balance of probabilities.

enrichment.short_title: He: POCA Part 5 interim receiving order upheld on money-transfer business
key_facts: The Assets Recovery Agency obtained an interim receiving order over Mr He's and his wife's property linked to Futsing Finance Ltd, a cash remittance business.
Police investigations had not charged Mr He, but production orders revealed large cash throughput, multiple property purchases and a Greek fraud conviction.
The interim receiver reported many clients could not explain remitted funds and a high proportion were asylum seekers working without authority.
Mr He argued Part 5 proceedings were criminal in nature, required criminal standard proof and were disproportionate; he sought discharge of the order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application to vary or discharge an interim receiving order under Part 5 Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 civil recovery provisions.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; interim receiving order continued subject to receiver reporting by 15 January 2005, with liberty to reapply if delayed.
enrichment.ratio: Part 5 POCA civil recovery proceedings are civil not criminal for Convention purposes; unlawful conduct is proved on the balance of probabilities under section 241(3), and an interim receiving order may continue while a good arguable case of recoverable property remains despite the receiver's interim concerns.
legal_issues: Whether Part 5 civil recovery engages Article 6 criminal protections
Standard of proof for unlawful conduct and interim receiving orders
Compatibility with Articles 7, 8 and Protocol 1 Article 1
Whether prior non-prosecution made civil recovery an abuse of process
Test for discharge or variation of an interim receiving order
linked_authorities: Engel v The Netherlands (No 1) [1976] 1 EHRR 647
Director of the Assets Recovery Agency v Walsh [2004] NIQB 21
R (Mudie) v Dover Magistrates' Court [2003] QB 1238

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme and human rights analysis are detailed; underlying criminality remained investigatory at interim stage.

notes: Tax treatment of ERA basic award in ECUA unfair dismissal consent order; s.148 termination payment exemption.

enrichment.short_title: Clayton: ECUA basic award after unfair dismissal held non-taxable termination payment
key_facts: Birmingham City Council terminated and re-employed 126 employees, including Clayton, to remove Essential Car User Allowance from contracts.
An employment tribunal found unfair dismissal and a consent order reinstated ECUA and ordered basic awards under section 119 ERA.
Clayton received £5,060 pursuant to the consent order and did not include it in his self-assessment.
HMRC amended the return; the General Commissioners and Patten J held the payment was a section 148 termination payment below the £30,000 threshold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Crown appeal to the Court of Appeal against High Court dismissal of an appeal on the tax treatment of an employment tribunal consent-order payment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the £5,060 payment was not taxable as an emolument or section 154 benefit but was a section 148 termination payment exempt below £30,000.
enrichment.ratio: A basic award paid pursuant to a genuine compromise after unfair dismissal is compensation for termination, not an emolument from continued employment under section 19; payments pursuant to an arm's-length bargain are not section 154 benefits, following Mairs v Haughey, and may fall within the section 148 termination payment exemption.
legal_issues: Whether reinstatement under section 114 treated the payment as emoluments from employment
Whether the payment was a taxable benefit under section 154 ICTA
Whether the payment was received in connection with termination under section 148
Effect of ET lack of jurisdiction to order basic award alongside reinstatement
linked_authorities: Mairs v Haughey (1992) 66 TC 273
Hochstrasser v Mayes [1960] AC 376
Shilton v Wilmshurst [1991] 1 AC 684

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis across sections 19, 148 and 154 is detailed and the appellate conclusion is explicit.

notes: Hackney carriage DSA taxi test policy; section 57 information request versus unlawful licence condition.

enrichment.short_title: Kaye: DSA taxi test policy lawful as fit-and-proper information under section 57
key_facts: Darlington Borough Council adopted a policy requiring hackney carriage drivers renewing licences to pass the Driving Standards Agency taxi test.
Malcolm Kaye, an experienced driver, refused to take the test and his licence renewal was refused in November 2003.
Magistrates upheld his appeal, treating the DSA requirement as an unlawful condition on grant of a licence.
The council appealed by case stated, relying on section 57 power to require information reasonably necessary to assess fitness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case stated appeal from magistrates' court upholding a hackney carriage driver's appeal against licence renewal refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to a fresh bench to rehear the appeal applying the council's lawful policy.
enrichment.ratio: A council may adopt a policy that drivers who have not passed the DSA taxi test are not fit and proper persons; requiring information of a pass certificate is a section 57 information request, not an unlawful condition on grant, and magistrates rehearing such appeals must apply the council's lawful policy.
legal_issues: Whether the DSA test requirement was a condition or a section 57 information request
Whether licensing authorities may require standards beyond the 12-month ordinary driving licence minimum
Application of Wathan v Neath on conditions attached to hackney carriage licences
How magistrates should approach rehearing appeals where a lawful council policy exists
linked_authorities: Wathan v Neath and Port Talbot County Borough Council [2002] EWHC 1634 (Admin)
Sagnata Investments Ltd v Norwich Corporation [1971] 2 QB 614
British Oxygen Co Ltd v Board of Trade [1971] AC 610

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme and policy-lawfulness analysis are clear; individual merits remitted to magistrates.
